name: s1: Simple test-time scaling
problem: OpenAI's o1 showed test-time scaling works but did not publish its methodology, and replication attempts were producing complicated systems.
mechanism: Two parts. (1) CURATE s1K: 1,000 questions paired with reasoning traces, selected on three criteria validated by ablations - difficulty, diversity, and quality. (2) BUDGET FORCING, the transferable mechanism: control test-time compute by FORCEFULLY TERMINATING the model's thinking process when a budget is exhausted, or by LENGTHENING it by appending 'Wait' multiple times to the generation when the model tries to end - which induces it to double-check and often fix incorrect reasoning steps. Then plain SFT of Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on s1K.
speedup_reported: s1-32B EXCEEDS o1-preview on competition math by up to 27% (MATH and AIME24). More important for this repo than the accuracy claim: scaling s1-32B WITH BUDGET FORCING allows EXTRAPOLATING BEYOND ITS PERFORMANCE WITHOUT TEST-TIME INTERVENTION, from 50% to 57% on AIME24. Budget forcing is thus a knob that moves the accuracy/OUTPUT-TOKEN frontier, and the operator sets the token budget explicitly.
notes:
ADOPTION: research-only as a system - model, data, and code are open (s1-32B weights released, which is unusual for this sub-area and is recorded as open_weights = true), but budget forcing is not a feature in any production engine. It is trivially implementable though: append 'Wait' and cap the trace, which is why it belongs in this slice despite being research-only. THE OPERATING-POINT POINT, which is the durable contribution for anyone reasoning about serving cost: budget forcing makes the ACCURACY-vs-TOKEN-COUNT relationship a directly controllable dial, so a serving system can trade latency for accuracy at a known token price. The append-'Wait' trick is also why reasoning-token counts became a first-class serving metric rather than an implementation detail.
